sections.heading: Rotational piezoelectric wind energy harvesting using impact-induced resonance

Ying Yang,,) Qinlong Shen,² Jiamei Jin,1 Yiping Wang,1 Wangjie Qian, and Dewang Yuan² 'State Key Laboratory of Mechanics and Control of Mechanical Structures, Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, PO Box 359, 29 Yudao Street, Nanjing, Jiangsu 210016, China 2School of Materials Science and Engineering, Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, 29 Yudao Street, Nanjing, Jiangsu 210016, China (Received 24 March 2014; accepted 26 June 2014; published online 5 August 2014) To improve the output power of a rotational piezoelectric wind energy harvester, impact-induced resonance is proposed to enable effective excitation of the piezoelectric cantilevers' vibration modes and obtain optimum deformation, which enhances the mechanical/electrical energy transformation. The impact force is introduced by forming a piezoelectric bimorph cantilever polygon that is fixed at the circumference of the rotating fan's internal surface. Elastic balls are placed inside the polygon. When wind rotates the device, the balls strike the piezoelectric cantilevers, and thus electricity is generated by the piezoelectric effect. The impact point is carefully chosen to use the first bending mode as much as possible, and thus maximize the harvesting eficiency. The design enables each bimorph to be struck in a similar area and every bimorph is struck in that area at different moments. As a result, a relatively stable output frequency can be obtained. The output frequency can also be changed by choosing different bimorph dimensions, which will also make the device simpler and the costs lower. A prototype piezoelectric energy harvester consisting of twelve piezoelectric cantilevers was constructed. The piezoelectric cantilevers were made from phosphor bronze, the lead zirconium titanate (PZT)-based bimorph cantilever had dimensions of $4 7 \mathrm { m m } \times 2 0 \mathrm { m m } \times 0 . 5 \mathrm { m m }$ , and the elastic balls were made from steel with a diameter of $1 0 \mathrm { m m }$ The optimal DC output power was $6 1 3 \mu \mathrm { W }$ across the $2 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ resistor at a rotation speed of $2 0 0 \mathrm { r / m i n }$ with an inscribed circle diameter of $3 1 \mathrm { m m }$ . $©$ 2014 AIP Publishing LLC. [http://dx.doi.org/10.1063/1.4887481] In recent years, advances in wireless technology and low-energy electronics have been accompanied by significantly increased research into energy harvesting systems, which can acquire ambient energy and convert it into usable electrical energy. One driving force behind this search for new energy harvesting devices is the desire to power sensor networks and mobile devices without using batteries.1-5 The generated energy can be used in low power wireless sensor systems that are either distributed extensively or located in polluted and/or dangerous areas. Wiring or battery replacement costs for the densely populated nodes in a network are usually very high, and some of these operations may even be prohibited by the infrastructure or the environment. As this technology continues to advance, energy harvesting is becoming an enabling technology that can provide "endless energy" throughout the lifespan of the electronics. The use of piezoelectric materials to capitalize on the ambient vibrations that surround a system is one method that has seen considerably increased usage for energy harvesting applications. Piezoelectric materials generate electrical energy when their shapes are distorted by forces, allowing these materials to easily produce high voltages with a relatively simple structure.24 However, it has been found that piezoelectric transducers are more suitable for kinetic to electrical energy conversion. In addition to the advantage of being smaller and lighter, the piezoelectric devices have higher energy densities when compared with their electrostatic and electromagnetic counterparts. When compared with the mechanical vibrations gathered from automobiles, walking, rotary machines, and water flow, wind is a far more attractive sourc electrical energy. Wnd isavailable everywhere, meaning that the technology can be implemented on a universal platform. Normal vibration sources in the environment are random and are thus difficult to control, but wind flow provi cnstant sourc mechanical energy.Priya al2,13 designed and optimized small-scale piezoelectric windmills to harvest electrical energy from wind energy using piezoelectric bimorph actuators. The structure and framework of their windmill was similar to that of a conventional windmill, except for its active piezoelectric blades. When the wind blows through the windmill, the active blades oscillate in turn and thus produce electricity. Wind-based electrical energy harvesting using piezoelectric bimorph transducers has significant advantages over other approaches. One of the challenges that is associated with small-scale electrical energy generation is obtaining output powers of more than $2 0 ~ \mathrm { m W }$ using smallsized vanes with surface areas of $2 { - } 5 \ \mathrm { i n } .$ 2 at wind speeds lower than $7 \mathrm { m p h }$ 12,13 However, it was found in a previously reported piezoelectric design that a certain amount of the power losses derived from sliding friction between the triangular clamps and the piezoelectric bimorph, which may result in lower lifetimes for the bimorphs and low momentum under low wind conditions. Umeda et al.14,15 proposed a mechanism that used mechanical impact to generate electrical power via piezoelectric transducers. A steel ball was used and was allowed to fall freely on to the center of a vibrator. The aim of this Letter is to present a rotational piezoelectric energy harvester in which impact-induced resonance is used to enable effective excitation of the intrinsic mode of vibration of piezoelectric cantilevers, and thus obtain optimum deformation, which will be beneficial for the mechanical/electrical energy transformation. The impact force is introduced through formation of a piezoelectric bimorph cantilever polygon, which is fixed at the circumference of the rotating fan's internal surface. Elastic balls are placed inside the polygon. When the wind causes the device to rotate, the balls will strike the piezoelectric cantilevers and thus electricity will be generated by the piezoelectric effect. In this Letter, piezoelectric bimorphs were chosen to be the energy-harvesting units. In addition, the impact force is used for the purposes of better performance and higher efficiency. Because it is known that an impact can excite resonance under any operating conditions, the impact of the balls on the cantilever can effectively excite its vibration mode and obtain the optimum deformation, which will be beneficial for the mechanical/electrical energy transformation. If the cantilever operates at a frequency that is close to its natural frequency, then the amplitude of the vibration will be enlarged to a maximum. A basic unit of the proposed impact-induced piezoelectric energy harvester, as shown in Fig. 1, consists of a piezoelectric bimorph cantilever and a free elastic ball. When the ball strikes the cantilever, the vibration of the piezoelectric cantilever produces electricity. The mechanical energy of the ball from free falling is redistributed into three parts: the first part goes to the cantilever, and this part of the energy will be converted into electricity; the second part is friction loss, and this part is very small because there is little contact to accompany the actual impact; the third part is the kinetic energy and the potential energy that is stored in the ball, and this energy will continue to be stored in the ball until the next impact. Figure 1(b) shows the experimentally measured characteristics of dropping height versus peak output voltage for various ball masses. It is easy to see that the impact of the ball on the cantilever is nearly a perfectly elastic collision. This basic unit will therefore have higher efficiency when it is used to construct a rotating piezoelectric energy harvester. The piezoelectric cantilevers are arranged in a polygon structure that describes the circumference of a circle. Elastic balls are then placed inside the polygon. When wind blows, the device will rotate, the balls will strike one of the piezoelectric cantilevers, and thus electricity will be generated. The wind energy will first change into the potential energy of the balls. The way that the balls strike the cantilever beam is similar to an impact force on the cantilever. This design offers the advantages of high efficiency and low wear and tear. Because an ideal impact force would excite all the vibration modes of a structure, the cantilever's response may contain all possible modes. Vibration from either the higher frequencies or unnecessary modes will limit the performance of the polygon-structured piezoelectric energy harvester by producing opposite charges or poor output power. To overcome this issue, this Letter introduces an enhanced rotational piezoelectric energy harvester that uses impact-induced resonance. It is known that the first bending mode produces the highest amplitude and power, and it was therefore decided to design the harvester to use the first bending mode as much as possible. To maximize the harvesting efficiency, the impact area is limited to a length of "1," as shown in Fig. 2. If "1" is carefully chosen so that the impact area lies near the peak of the first bending mode, then the vibration frequency will be close to the first bending mode frequency. The length of "1" can be reduced by increasing the number of bimorphs used. If the generator is assembled such that "1" is sufficiently small, each bimorph will be struck in identical or very similar areas, although at different moments. As a result, a relatively stable output frequency can be obtained. In addition, the output frequency can be controlled by careful selection of the various dimensions of the bimorph. Obviously, more than one ball can be placed in the polygon for better performance. The total number of balls used can be optimized for improved output performance. ![](images/6681ac31dfbbf6a5b5dbb83eac684ecfd8d535b8e2162cedff91a61f4215e02a.jpg) FIG. 1. A prototype harvester is shown in Fig. 3; the prototype was fabricated with the geometrical properties listed in Table I. A series of experiments was carried out to investigate the effectiveness of the proposed device at various rotation speeds. The number of elastic balls was adjusted so that the fan could be rotated easily under normal wind flow conditions. The output voltage was monitored on an HP 54601A digital four-channel oscilloscope using an HP 10071A probe. The relationship among the number of elastic balls used, the rotation speed and the load dependence of the rectified output DC voltage was investigated experimentally. The rectification circuit that was used was a typical full wave bridge rectifier. It was found that the output voltages for ball numbers 111 all reach their peaks at rotation speeds of around $2 0 0 \mathrm { r / m i n }$ and the optimum ball number is seven. Figure 4 shows the signal waveform generated from the harvester with 7 balls inside and at the rotating speed of $2 0 0 \mathrm { r / m i n }$ measured. Figure 5 shows the rectified voltage with seven balls inside the rectifier under various loads. The output DClike voltages are considered to be useful as a power source for low-power electronics. The output power was measured across the load, which is connected in parallel to a full bridge rectifier and a capacitor. Figure 6 shows the DC-like output power generated by a harvester containing seven balls and operating at a rotational speed of $2 0 0 \mathrm { r / m i n }$ when measured across various resistive loads. The optimal DC output power was $6 1 3 \mu \mathrm { W }$ across the $2 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ resistor with an inscribed circle diameter of $3 1 \mathrm { m m }$ . In conclusion, this Letter demonstrates a methodology for ball-impact-induced resonance to enable power to be harnessed from freely available wind on a small scale. The piezoelectric wind energy harvester was designed based on the knowledge that an impact can excite resonance under any operating conditions. A rotational piezoelectric energy harvester has been presented and impact-induced resonance was used to enable effective excitation of the intrinsic mode of vibration of the piezoelectric cantilevers to obtain optimum deformation, which will be beneficial for the mechanical/ electrical energy transformation. The first bending mode of vibration was deliberately chosen so that the impact area was located near the peak of the first bending mode; the vibration frequency was thus close to the first bending mode frequency, and this maximized the harvesting efficiency. The impact force was introduced through the formation of a piezoelectric bimorph cantilever polygon, which was fixed at the circumference of the rotating fan's internal surface. Elastic balls were placed inside the polygon. When the wind rotated the device, the balls struck the piezoelectric cantilevers and thus electricity was generated via the piezoelectric effect. A prototype wind energy harvester was built, and its properties were measured and optimized experimentally. The optimal DC output power was $6 1 3 \mu \mathrm { W }$ across the $2 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ resistor at a rotation speed of $2 0 0 \mathrm { r / m i n }$ with an inscribed circle diameter of $3 1 \mathrm { m m }$ . The generated electricity can be stored in a supercapacitor and can be used to power wireless sensors in remote locations. ![](images/70288497debd440409bf30b3c5b6f514f27eb74ce7409e227cca7689a9724b1c.jpg) FIG. 5.
